nameStory: The 'small-leaved plantain lily' gets its name from its compact foliage compared to its bigger hosta cousins, and its lily-like flowers that bloom on tall stalks. The 'plantain' part comes from the broad, ribbed leaves that reminded early botanists of the common plantain weed, though they're completely unrelated plants.
description: Small-leaved plantain lily is a clumping perennial garden plant that forms neat mounds of heart-shaped leaves with prominent parallel veins running from base to tip. Originally from Japan, this hosta can spread up to 4 feet across, creating dense colonies of foliage that stay green all summer. In mid-summer, it sends up tall flower spikes topped with tubular pink to purple blooms that attract hummingbirds and bees.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with smooth edges and 3-5 prominent parallel veins that feel like raised cords when you run your finger along them. Leaves may be solid green, lime green, or have white edges or center stripes depending on the variety.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tubular flowers in shades of pink to purple cluster at the top of leafless stalks that rise 2-3 feet above the foliage. Each flower is about an inch long and slightly fragrant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, symmetrical clumps that expand outward each year through underground roots. The entire plant has a fountain-like appearance with leaves arching outward from the center.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After flowering, develops papery seed capsules that split open to reveal flat, black, paper-thin seeds that rustle in the wind.

habitat: Found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like gardens, parks, and around homes where it has been planted as an ornamental. Thrives in partial to full shade and rich, moist soil. Occasionally escapes cultivation to establish in nearby wooded edges or disturbed areas with similar growing conditions.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as tightly rolled shoots that unfurl into fresh green foliage. Look for the distinctive parallel leaf veins as leaves expand.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when both foliage and flowers are present. Blooms typically appear from mid-July through mid-August on tall stalks above the leaves.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow and begin to die back after first frost. Dried flower stalks with papery seed capsules may persist into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. Only the crown at soil level survives, often marked by dried leaf remnants.

funFact: Hostas are considered a delicacy in Japan where young shoots are harvested and eaten as a spring vegetable called 'urui' - they taste similar to asparagus with a slightly mucilaginous texture!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other hosta species, but small-leaved plantain lily is generally more compact than blue plantain lily and has smaller leaves than Siebold's plantain lily. The key is checking the overall plant size and leaf proportions - this species rarely exceeds 4 feet across.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'plantain lily,' this plant is neither a true lily nor related to the plantain herb. It's actually in the asparagus family, which explains why the young shoots are edible and taste somewhat like asparagus.
compareHints: Among New England hostas, small-leaved plantain lily is the most compact species with proportionally smaller leaves than blue plantain lily or Siebold's plantain lily. Unlike scented hosta which has pure white fragrant flowers, this species has pink to purple blooms. The narrow-leaved plantain lily has much more lance-shaped leaves rather than the heart-shaped leaves of small-leaved plantain lily.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue Plantain-lily stands out from other hostas by its blue-green leaf color and substantial, waxy texture.
Scented hosta is the only fragrant species among all hostas - this alone sets it apart from blue plantain-lily, Siebold's plantain lily, and other relatives.
Among hostas, this species is unmistakable due to its narrow leaves - all other common New England hostas have much broader, heart-shaped or oval foliage.
Siebold's Plantain Lily stands out from other hostas by its exceptional size and that distinctive blue-gray, waxy leaf texture.
